title: Romeo and Juliet's Borrowed Plot
objective: After this level you can explain why Shakespeare borrowed his plots and what he added to them, using Romeo and Juliet.
summary: Romeo and Juliet came from Arthur Brooke's 1562 poem, with Ovid's Pyramus and Thisbe behind it. Borrowing was normal; Shakespeare's changes (four days, Mercutio, sympathy) made it his.

cards.headline: Shakespeare gives away the ending before the play begins.
cards.body: Romeo and Juliet opens with a Prologue announcing that "A pair of star-cross'd lovers take their life". No twist, no surprise: you know how it ends before anyone has fallen in love. So why would a crowd stay to watch?

cards.headline: A borrowed story
cards.body: Shakespeare wrote Romeo and Juliet about 1594 to 1596. His main source was Arthur Brooke's long poem The Tragicall Historye of Romeus and Juliet (1562), itself based on a French version of an Italian tale by Matteo Bandello. Further back stands Ovid's Pyramus and Thisbe from Level 7, one inspiration for the play, which Shakespeare also turned into a farce in A Midsummer Night's Dream.

cards.headline: Nobody wanted a new plot
cards.body: That wasn't cheating. Playwrights of the time weren't too bothered about being original: they reworked old stories and even used other people's plots. With a few exceptions, Shakespeare didn't invent the plots of his plays. The question wasn't what happens. It was how well you could tell it.
cards.callout: Borrowing plots was normal; the telling was the craft.

cards.headline: What he added
cards.body: Put the versions side by side. Brooke's story takes at least nine months; Shakespeare crams it into four days, Sunday to Thursday morning. In Brooke, Mercutio is just a guest at Capulet's feast; Shakespeare gives him the Queen Mab speech, the jokes and his death. And Brooke's preface condemns the lovers as a warning to youth who neglect their parents' authority. Shakespeare doesn't follow his lead.

learned: Borrowing plots was normal for playwrights

questions.prompt: Put the versions of the story in order, from oldest to newest.
items: An Italian tale by Matteo Bandello
questions.explanation: Matteo Bandello's Italian tale came first, then a French version of it, then Arthur Brooke's long poem (1562), and finally Shakespeare's Romeo and Juliet.

questions.prompt: Why was Shakespeare happy to borrow the plot of Romeo and Juliet?

options.label: Copyright law made him credit Brooke
options.rationale: Nothing in the level mentions such a law.

options.label: Playwrights then reworked old stories as a matter of course
Audiences refused to watch new stories
options.rationale: The point is that originality wasn't expected, not banned.

options.label: Brooke hired him to adapt the poem
options.rationale: Nothing in the level says so.

questions.explanation: Playwrights of his time weren't bothered about originality and reworked old stories; with a few exceptions Shakespeare didn't invent his plots.

questions.prompt: Level 7's Pyramus and Thisbe was one inspiration for Romeo and Juliet. What do the two stories share?

options.label: Forbidden young lovers who both take their own lives
A mulberry tree whose fruit turns purple
A comic workman who plays a wall
options.rationale: That's Shakespeare's farce version in A Midsummer Night's Dream.

options.label: A happy wedding at the end
options.rationale: Both end in the lovers' deaths.

questions.explanation: Ovid's Babylonian lovers are forbidden to marry and both die by their own hands, as Shakespeare's star-crossed lovers do.
